High-School Cybersecurity Standards & Instructional Design Evidence¶

Professional analysis of the 51-jurisdiction standards matrix¶

Version 2.0 · August 6, 2026

This notebook turns the supplied workbook into a reproducible decision analysis for curriculum design, state localization, teacher implementation, product positioning, and pilot evaluation. It answers:

  1. What cybersecurity knowledge and skills are expected of high-school students?
  2. Which standards recur across jurisdictions?
  3. Which state-specific standards or approval conditions require supplemental content?
  4. Which teaching strategies improve knowledge, application, retention, and transfer?
  5. What evidence exists specifically for K–12 cybersecurity instruction?
  6. What broader STEM and learning-science evidence can reasonably be transferred?
  7. Which course structures are feasible for teachers without deep cybersecurity backgrounds?
  8. What device, network, privacy, and safety constraints affect hands-on work?
  9. What do existing products cover, and what do they leave underserved?
  10. What outcomes can be measured during a pilot?

Interpretation boundary. The workbook is a planning and source inventory, not a completed 51-jurisdiction legal crosswalk. Exact state expectations are decomposed for seven jurisdictions. Cross-jurisdiction recurrence is therefore reported only for the explicit high-school subset of those seven jurisdictions, with the denominator shown throughout.

What was improved from the first notebook¶

The first version was directionally useful and executed cleanly, but several important conclusions were manually authored rather than calculated. This revision makes the analysis more defensible and professional by:

  • restricting state recurrence analysis to explicit high-school exact expectations;
  • foregrounding data completeness and denominators before presenting findings;
  • applying an auditable, multi-label cybersecurity-domain taxonomy across state, national, and AP records;
  • distinguishing literal standard identifiers from normalized concepts that can be compared across frameworks;
  • replacing broad keyword flags with field-specific evidence excerpts and an explicit “screening, not legal finding” label;
  • separating direct K–12 cybersecurity evidence from transferable STEM and learning-science evidence;
  • deriving course feasibility from the workbook's lesson and time models;
  • coding the sampled product matrix with a transparent capability rubric rather than asserting a market-wide gap;
  • converting the pilot section into a measurement plan, analysis protocol, data template, and decision framework; and
  • exporting the underlying analytical tables so every chart and recommendation can be audited.
Workbook: Foundations_of_Cybersecurity_51_Jurisdiction_Standards_Matrix(1) (1).xlsx
Output directory: /mnt/data/cybersecurity_analysis_outputs

The workbook inventories all 51 jurisdictions, but only 7 have decomposed high-school expectations. All recurrence results below therefore use n=7: Alabama, California, Florida, Louisiana, New York, North Dakota, Ohio.

2. Expected high-school cybersecurity knowledge and skills¶

Frameworks rarely use identical identifiers or strand names. To compare them responsibly, the analysis applies a transparent multi-label taxonomy to the verbatim state expectations, national standards, and AP learning objectives. A record may map to more than one domain, so column totals do not sum to the number of records.

Taxonomy audit result
All 183 benchmarking records received at least one domain assignment; 0 were unmatched. Assignments are rule-based and multi-label. They should be reviewed when the workbook adds new wording or frameworks.

Answer: expected high-school profile
The standards describe more than awareness. Students are expected to explain and compare systems, apply and configure controls, analyze risks and evidence, investigate problems, create artifacts, and justify decisions within authorized and ethical boundaries. The strongest common-state spine in the exact subset consists of: Security foundations, risk & controls, Threats, vulnerabilities & social engineering, Data protection, privacy & cryptography, Networks, cloud & IoT security, Identity & access management. National and AP frameworks add depth in incident response, governance, system hardening, communication, and selected secure-software practices.

3. Which standards recur across jurisdictions?¶

Literal state identifiers do not recur because jurisdictions organize standards differently. The defensible comparison is therefore concept recurrence after normalization, not a claim that states adopted the same wording.

Answer: recurring standards spine
5 normalized domains appear in a majority of the 7 exact-state high-school subsets: Security foundations, risk & controls (6/7); Threats, vulnerabilities & social engineering (6/7); Data protection, privacy & cryptography (6/7); Networks, cloud & IoT security (4/7); Identity & access management (4/7). Less frequent in this limited subset are: Governance, ethics, law & safe use (3/7); Computing systems, devices & hardening (3/7); Monitoring, incident response & resilience (2/7); Secure software, scripting & automation (2/7); Communication, collaboration & careers (0/7). These lower counts should not be interpreted as low importance: national and AP frameworks add substantial depth, and 44 jurisdictions have not yet been decomposed.

4. State-specific standards and approval conditions requiring supplemental content¶

Two different localization problems must be managed separately:

  1. Content localization — exact identifiers, named-course or CTE outcomes, state privacy/digital-citizenship requirements, AI-related expectations, credentials, or work-based learning.
  2. Approval localization — course code and credit, instructional time, teacher assignment, pathway filing, assessment rules, facilities, privacy, accessibility, district security, acceptable use, and governance.

Answer: supplemental content and approval conditions
The largest research need is exact extraction for 44 jurisdictions. The workbook also identifies 22 jurisdictions in named-course or CTE-overlay classifications, and explicit high-school AI/cyber expectations in Alabama, North Dakota. Approval cannot be inferred from standards alignment alone: each filing needs evidence for course code/credit, teacher assignment, instructional time, pathway/Perkins treatment when applicable, assessments or credentials, facilities and network controls, privacy, accessibility, acceptable use, district security, AI governance, and evaluation.

5. Teaching strategies and the evidence base¶

The evidence must be stratified by directness. K–12 cybersecurity studies are most relevant but relatively small and heterogeneous. Broader STEM and learning-science findings are stronger in several areas, but they should be transferred only when the learning mechanism and classroom conditions match.

8
Workbook pedagogy practices
Research-grounded design practices in the supplied workbook
6
Workbook research sources
Cybersecurity and curriculum-alignment sources supplied
Pedagogy evidence register supplied in the workbook
Practice Evidence synthesis Course design rule Evidence strength / caveat
Scenario-first, problem-centered instruction Systematic and design literature supports authentic, contextual problems; the supplied high-school guideline and AP framework consistently organize knowledge around decisions and scenarios. Open each module with a consequential scenario; end with an evidence-backed decision or artifact. Moderate; outcome studies remain heterogeneous.
Scaffolded hands-on labs in isolated environments Quasi-experimental and virtual-lab studies report knowledge and self-efficacy gains; cyber-range/game reviews warn that engagement alone is not mastery. Use concept briefing → modeled example → guided lab → independent variation → explanation; never target public systems. Moderate for proximal learning; limited long-term/transfer evidence.
CTF and games as retrieval/application, not the entire course CTFs can increase interest and provide authentic problem solving, while reviews find uneven learning design and shallow conceptual coverage in many games. Use short challenges after instruction and a capstone competition; score reasoning, evidence, and reflection in addition to flags. Promising but mixed.
Authentic performance assessment Course and CTE quality standards emphasize observable competencies, aligned assessment, feedback, and real-world application. Require logs, diagrams, code, policies, incident timelines, and briefings with analytic rubrics. Strong design consensus; cyber-specific causal evidence is limited.
Spaced retrieval, interleaving, and delayed retention General learning science strongly supports retrieval and spacing; the high-school cyber evidence base rarely measures delayed retention. Use cumulative checks every module, mixed-domain labs every four modules, and a delayed post-course measure. Strong general evidence; cyber-specific implementation evidence needed.
Collaborative roles plus individual accountability Cyber learning is collaborative, but group-composition effects can alter self-efficacy and interest. Rotate analyst, operator, recorder, and briefer roles; collect an individual explanation from every student. Moderate.
Low floor, high ceiling, and belonging-centered design CSTA/AI4K12 and pathway guidance prioritize inclusive collaboration, accessible entry points, relevant contexts, and belonging. Provide novice path, extension path, multiple artifact formats, accessible labs, and culturally relevant scenarios without lowering standards. Strong expert consensus; measure subgroup outcomes.
Teacher enablement and stable lab operations Program-quality and online-course standards identify professional development, support, usability, and technology reliability as implementation conditions. Provide prebuilt environments, troubleshooting trees, answer keys, misconception notes, safety scripts, and implementation rehearsals. Strong implementation consensus.

Broader STEM and learning-science evidence that can reasonably inform course design
Principle Evidence base Reasonable transfer Boundary Source
Retrieval practice Yang et al. (2021): meta-analysis of 222 studies and 48,478 students; overall classroom benefit g≈0.50. Frequent low-stakes recall, cumulative checks, and retrieval before re-teaching. Retrieval strengthens accessible memory; it does not replace authentic application or transfer tasks. https://doi.org/10.1037/bul0000309
Distributed practice / spacing Cepeda et al. (2006): quantitative synthesis of 317 experiments; later classroom review also reports a moderate benefit. Revisit identity, network, risk, and incident concepts across modules and include delayed checks. Spacing schedule should match the intended retention interval; simple repetition is insufficient. https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.132.3.354
Worked examples and scaffold fading Atkinson et al. (2000): review of worked-example research in problem solving. Model one complete analysis or configuration, guide a second, then fade prompts for an independent variant. Students must explain decisions and eventually solve without the template. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543070002181
Guided inquiry Lazonder & Harmsen (2016): meta-analysis showing that guidance materially supports inquiry learning. Use bounded questions, safe datasets, hints, checkpoints, and reflection in labs. Unguided discovery is a poor default for novice learners and non-specialist teachers. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654315627366
Inquiry-based science instruction Furtak et al. (2012): meta-analysis of 37 K–12 studies; mean effect around 0.50, with teacher guidance important. Organize investigations around evidence, explanation, and justified decisions—not tool manipulation alone. Cybersecurity tasks must still be explicitly authorized, isolated, and technically supported. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654312457206
Active learning Freeman et al. (2014): 225 undergraduate STEM studies; average exam improvement about 0.47 SD. Use explanation, peer reasoning, prediction, troubleshooting, and short practice throughout instruction. The population is higher education; use as design support, not direct K–12 cyber proof. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1319030111
Formative feedback Wisniewski et al. (2020): meta-analysis of 435 studies; average effect around d=0.48 with substantial heterogeneity. Give timely, task-specific feedback on reasoning, evidence, configurations, and revision. Praise or scores alone are weaker than actionable information tied to the task and next step. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2019.03087
Transfer through comparison and reflection How People Learn II synthesizes evidence that transfer improves when learners compare cases, use models, and reflect on when knowledge applies. Change scenario surface features, ask students to select methods, contrast solutions, and justify adaptation. Retention measures alone cannot substantiate far transfer. https://doi.org/10.17226/24783

Outcome Primary teaching strategy Cybersecurity-specific evidence Transferable evidence Confidence Pilot measure
Knowledge Scenario-first explicit teaching; vocabulary; worked examples; concept maps K–12 cyber studies support proximal knowledge gains from structured hands-on instruction. Worked examples, active learning, and feedback Moderate Parallel standards-aligned pre/post assessment
Application Modeled → guided → independent isolated labs; authentic artifacts and rubrics Direct school studies support guided labs, but samples are small. Guided inquiry, formative feedback, deliberate practice Moderate Common performance tasks scored with analytic rubrics

Autonomy, relevance, collaborative learning Promising but mixed Interest/belonging plus learning measures—not engagement alone

Cognitive load and implementation-support principles Practice-grounded Prep time, fidelity checks, support tickets, lesson completion
Answer: evidence-based teaching model
Use scenario-first explicit instruction, worked examples, scaffolded isolated labs, authentic artifacts, timely feedback, and cumulative retrieval. For retention, space and revisit core concepts; for transfer, change scenario features, compare cases, fade scaffolds, and require students to select and justify methods. Use CTFs and games as application or retrieval—not as the entire curriculum. The direct K–12 cyber evidence is promising but still too limited to claim durable transfer without a delayed and novel-task pilot measure.

6. Course structures feasible for non-specialist teachers¶

Feasibility depends on a stable instructional routine, protected setup/assessment time, safe preconfigured environments, and teacher-facing diagnostics. The workbook's course architecture contains 20 modules, 60 lessons, and 3,300 core minutes.

Safety Authorization script, safe-target rules, prohibited actions, incident escalation path
Instruction Facilitation notes, worked example, checks for understanding, pacing options
Troubleshooting Decision tree organized by symptom, screenshot/log examples, escalation threshold
Assessment Rubric, answer key, calibration examples, feedback language, reassessment path
Differentiation Low-floor entry, accessibility supports, multilingual vocabulary, extensions
Professional learning Short rehearsal, sandbox access, office hours/community, update notices
Answer: feasible course structure
The most defensible default is the daily-semester model: 60 core lesson periods plus 30 periods for setup, extended labs, assessment, reteaching, interruption recovery, and capstone work. The 55-hour compressed model has no buffer and should be offered only where local policy permits and the implementation deliberately narrows variation. Block or 90-hour models provide more robust practice time. A repeated routine and strong teacher package are more important to non-specialist feasibility than adding more content.

7. Device, network, privacy, accessibility, and safety constraints¶

Hands-on cybersecurity is feasible in schools only when technical design is treated as a governed instructional system. The workbook's approval checklist identifies the core controls; the lab-mode matrix translates them into implementation choices.

Operational controls derived from the approval checklist
ID Category Required evidence Required operating decision
10 Facilities Device specifications, virtualization, cyber range, software, network isolation, egress controls Choose device floor, virtualization/range mode, isolation, reset, and egress design before procurement.
12 Student privacy FERPA, COPPA, state student-data law, DPA, retention/deletion, subprocessors Minimize accounts and student data; document retention, deletion, subprocessors, and vendor access.
13 Accessibility WCAG 2.2 AA, Section 504, ADA, captions, keyboard access, assistive-technology evidence Validate keyboard access, captions, screen-reader flow, color-independent cues, and alternatives.
14 Licensing and AUP Software licenses, acceptable use, authorization, safe-target rules, vulnerability disclosure Use only licensed tools and explicitly authorized targets; publish the lab compact and disclosure rules.
15 District IT/security Security review, firewall/allowlist, account provisioning, incident escalation, isolation Pre-approve allowlists, firewall/proxy behavior, provisioning, logging, and escalation with district IT.
16 AI and integrity Approved AI uses, student-data limits, attribution, human validation, academic integrity Define approved AI uses, prohibited data, attribution, verification, and integrity expectations.
17 Equity and access Multilingual learner supports, accommodations, offline/low-bandwidth alternative, inclusive examples Provide low-bandwidth/offline alternatives and equivalent learning paths for device constraints.
18 Parent transparency Syllabus/material access, consent/notice, opt-out or alternative activity where required Make the syllabus, tools, data practices, and alternative activities visible to families where required.
Lab-mode decision matrix
Lab mode Device burden Network/IT burden Privacy posture Safety posture Best fit No-go condition
Approved browser-hosted range Low–medium; modern browser Medium–high: allowlists, ports, proxies, certificates, identity Vendor accounts/telemetry require review Strong when tenant and targets are isolated and resettable 1:1 devices; districts able to approve a vendor No approved data agreement, blocked traffic, or unclear tenant isolation
Local VM or container image High: RAM, storage, virtualization/admin rights Low–medium after image distribution Can minimize external data transfer Strong when host-only networks, snapshots, least privilege, and reset are enforced Labs needing richer system/network control Virtualization disabled, unmanaged images, or any route to production systems
Offline simulation / packet capture / emulator Low–medium Low; can work without live egress Minimal account/data exposure Very strong for introductory analysis; no live target required Shared devices, filtered networks, fallback or accessibility path Used as the only mode when objectives require real configuration and troubleshooting
Hands-on launch gate
Go/no-go control Minimum condition before hands-on launch
Authorization Every activity identifies authorized targets, allowed actions, prohibited actions, and stop conditions.
Isolation No scanning, exploitation, credential use, or configuration changes against public or district production systems.
Identity and privacy Use synthetic data and least-privilege accounts; do not use real student passwords, secrets, or sensitive records.
Reset and recovery Each environment is resettable; known-good state and recovery instructions are documented.
Visibility and escalation Teacher/district personnel can identify failures, logs, and suspected misuse and know who to contact.
Accessibility and equity An equivalent path exists for students who cannot use virtualization, home internet, or a specific interface.
Answer: constraints affecting hands-on work
The largest constraints are not the cybersecurity concepts themselves; they are device capability, virtualization/admin rights, filtering and egress, account provisioning, vendor data practices, accessibility, safe-target authorization, environment reset, and district incident escalation. A professional product should support at least two modes—an approved browser range and an offline/isolated alternative—so schools can preserve the learning objective when local infrastructure differs.

Answer: product coverage and underserved bundle
The sampled routes collectively cover rigorous academic frameworks, hosted curricula, ranges, networking pathways, competitions, professional development, and credential signals. The capabilities least established in the workbook sample are: Exact, versioned state overlays, Offline or isolated lab alternative, Pilot outcome analytics, District/state approval evidence pack. The defensible product opportunity is therefore a bundled, semester-ready foundation with exact and version-controlled state overlays, filing artifacts, strong teacher enablement, safe flexible lab modes, privacy/accessibility governance, and pilot-ready analytics. This is an inference from six sampled routes—not a claim that no provider offers any individual feature.

9. Pilot outcomes, measurement plan, and analysis protocol¶

A pilot should test learning, transfer, implementation, safety, technical reliability, equity, and approval readiness. Satisfaction and completion are useful implementation indicators but are not substitutes for evidence of learning.

Professional pilot measurement plan
Outcome family Instrument / evidence Timing Unit Primary analysis Decision rule guidance
Knowledge — overall and by domain Parallel standards-aligned assessment with domain subscores Pre, post, delayed Student Paired mean change, 95% CI, paired effect size; item/domain diagnostics Pre-register a positive-change gate and minimum domain coverage; do not use normalized gain as the sole statistic
Application Two common performance tasks: e.g., risk/control analysis and network/incident task Midpoint and capstone Student/task Rubric means, proficiency rate, revision gain; double-score a sample Pre-register proficiency standard and acceptable inter-rater reliability
Delayed retention Parallel knowledge form plus selected repeated task elements 4–8 weeks after instruction/course Student Delayed score and retained proportion of post-minus-pre gain Pre-register an acceptable retention range and report uncertainty
Transfer Novel scenario with changed surface features requiring method selection and justification Capstone or delayed Student Analytic rubric: representation, evidence, method choice, mitigation, justification Require reasoning and adaptation; do not count a rehearsed replica as transfer
Safety and ethics Authorization/privacy scenario items; lab compact; incident and near-miss log Continuous Student/class Decision accuracy, violations, near misses, corrective actions Zero unauthorized targeting; every near miss reviewed and closed
Self-efficacy, interest, belonging Brief validated or carefully piloted scales plus open response Pre, midpoint, post Student Change and subgroup patterns; reliability of scale Secondary outcome only; never substitute for knowledge/performance
Engagement and completion Attendance, lesson completion, attempts, revisions, time-on-task Continuous Student/class Rates, distributions, relationship to learning outcomes Use diagnostically; high engagement without learning is not success
Teacher feasibility Preparation minutes, troubleshooting minutes, support contacts, confidence, fidelity checklist Weekly and post Teacher/lesson Median and trend by module; completion and deviation reasons Pre-register a sustainable prep/support target after initial onboarding
Technical reliability Login, launch, reset, blocked traffic, device failure, uptime, IT escalation Each lab Session/class Launch success, failure rate, time lost, root-cause categories Pre-register launch and uptime targets; no unresolved critical security issue
Equity and accessibility Access failures, accommodations, equivalent-path use, subgroup growth and experience Continuous/post Student/subgroup Disaggregated outcomes with small-cell suppression; missingness review No systematic access barrier; equivalent path must preserve the learning objective
Approval readiness Completed standards map, checklist evidence, safety/privacy artifacts, version register Before and after pilot Jurisdiction/site Percent resolved; unresolved stop conditions No marketing or approval claim while a stop condition remains unresolved
Cost and scalability Licenses, devices, PD/support hours, IT setup, reusable effort, cost per completer End of pilot Site/course Total and marginal cost; sensitivity by class size and lab mode Pre-register acceptable total cost and support burden for scale
Pilot data-template notes
Field Definition Type
student_id_hash Pseudonymous student identifier; never store names in the analysis file Text
assessment_wave pre, post, delayed, midpoint, or task Categorical
knowledge_total Common knowledge assessment score on a documented scale Numeric
*_score Domain or construct subscore with score range in a separate instrument codebook Numeric

Created: /mnt/data/Pilot_Measurement_Plan.csv
Created: /mnt/data/Pilot_Student_Data_Template.csv
Recommended pilot analysis protocol
Step Pre-registered analysis protocol
1 Lock instruments, rubrics, inclusion rules, primary outcomes, and decision gates before analyzing outcomes.
2 Score knowledge by total and domain; report paired change, uncertainty, and paired effect size.
3 Double-score at least a planned sample of performance and transfer artifacts; report agreement/reliability.
4 Use delayed and novel tasks to distinguish immediate recall from retention and transfer.
5 Analyze classrooms/sites explicitly; with multiple classes, use clustered or multilevel methods rather than treating every observation as independent.
6 Report attrition and missingness by wave; do not silently analyze only completers.
7 Disaggregate cautiously, suppress small cells, and frame subgroup comparisons as exploratory unless powered and pre-specified.
8 Triangulate learning with fidelity, teacher burden, technical reliability, safety events, and access barriers.
Answer: measurable pilot outcomes
At minimum, measure standards-aligned knowledge, two common performance tasks, delayed retention, and one genuinely novel transfer task. Pair those outcomes with safety/ethics decisions, teacher preparation and troubleshooting time, lab launch reliability, access and accommodation data, approval-evidence completion, and cost. Use paired change with uncertainty, analytic rubrics, inter-rater checks, and classroom-aware analysis. Pre-register local decision gates rather than adopting arbitrary universal pass thresholds.

Professional conclusion
The revised analysis supports a broad, performance-oriented high-school cybersecurity foundation, but it also makes the evidence boundary explicit: the cross-state recurrence sample is seven jurisdictions, direct K–12 intervention evidence is still limited, and the product matrix is sampled. The most defensible next step is a teacher-friendly semester pilot with exact state overlays, dual-mode safe labs, common performance tasks, delayed retention, novel transfer, and implementation metrics collected from the first lesson.

Reproducibility and claim controls¶

  • Workbook tables are read from Excel row 5, where the true headers begin.
  • Every quantitative standards result is generated from the supplied workbook.
  • The domain and performance-demand taxonomies are explicit rule sets in the notebook and are exported for audit.
  • Multi-label counts can exceed the number of records; they indicate coverage, not mutually exclusive categories.
  • “Exact-state recurrence” refers only to explicit high-school expectations in Alabama, California, Florida, Louisiana, New York, North Dakota, and Ohio.
  • State screening flags prioritize research and filing work; they are not legal conclusions.
  • External evidence tables contain direct source URLs and distinguish K–12 cyber-specific evidence from transferable evidence.
  • The product analysis describes six representative routes in the workbook and should not be marketed as a complete market census.
  • Pilot decision gates should be pre-registered locally after reviewing score scales, policy requirements, risk tolerance, and sample size.
